spans.assertion: hierarchical Poisson regression was used to investigate skin tone bias and referee prejudice associated with red cards across the games in the data set

after controlling for height, weight, age, goals scored, league country, and position, and adjusting for games played, skin tone bias still existed: darker-skin-rated players received more red cards on average than lighter-skin-rated players
red cards received were also related to the average level of prejudice in the referee's home country, independent of the player's skin tone
no evidence was found that referee prejudice interacted with player's skin tone to influence red cards received
darker skin tone soccer players receive more red cards relative to lighter skin tone players
average referee-home-country prejudice levels do not appear to play a role in the skin tone bias
hierarchical logistic regression was originally pursued as the strategy for both research questions
a large number of players had never received a red card and very few had received multiple red cards
dichotomizing the red card variable seemed an appropriate approach to test whether ever receiving a red card was related to skin tone rating
the original dichotomized logistic-regression strategy was altered/abandoned based on initial participant feedback
Poisson regression using the count of red cards as the outcome variable was used instead
Poisson regression was considered superior because it retained variability information that dichotomizing would have lost
technical limitations prohibited pursuing what was believed to be the optimal strategy for the second research question
mixed effects analysis with player and referee as level-2 variables was the preferred approach for research question 2
mixed effects modeling would have been an ideal strategy for addressing non-independence in the data
the mixed effects analysis could not be completed: available processing power was limited and on multiple attempts the computer overheated and shut down
the strategy outlined for research question 2 was used instead, believed viable but suboptimal
Poisson regression with games entered as an exposure (offset) variable was used to investigate associations between predictors and total red cards received
direct red cards were used as the outcome variable
yellow-red cards were not used as the outcome variable
direct red cards were chosen because they represent a more direct, subjective referee evaluation more likely to tap referee bias than yellow-reds
the analytical approach allowed investigation of each predictor's effect on observed red cards per player
including games as an exposure variable made the outcome a rate (red cards per game) rather than a count, addressing differences in opportunities to receive a red card
all analyses were completed using R (version 3.1.0)
the analysis followed Poisson regression methodology from UCLA (2014) and Penn State (2014), with additional guidance from Field, Miles, & Field (2012)
Poisson regression was determined the most appropriate technique for the research question
care was taken to follow reliable resources, cite sources, and explain analysis steps in detail

spans.note: Caveat that the project lacks typical peer review, so readers should scrutinize the approach before drawing strong conclusions

spans.assertion: data was aggregated at the individual player level (N=2053) prior to removing cases with missing data
effects of interest are presented as odds ratios with confidence intervals indicating percentage increase in red-card rate associated with predictors

spans.note: Pointer stating results by research question follow in subsections

spans.assertion: reliability across the two skin tone raters for each player was high (α = 0.96)
the two skin tone ratings were averaged into an overall skin tone index (M=0.29, SD=0.29)
player position was recoded into five dichotomous dummy variables: Forward (n=349), Midfielder (n=598), Fullback (n=543), Goalkeeper (n=196), and Other/NA (n=367)
position was collapsed into these categories rather than by field side to keep controls manageable, since red-card propensity was expected to differ by primary position but not field side
dichotomous dummy variables were created for the four league countries: England (reference, n=564), France (n=533), Germany (n=489), Spain (n=467)
player age was calculated as years from birth date to an arbitrarily selected reference date of January 1, 2013
additional transformations were made to the implicit and explicit prejudice variables for research question 2, detailed in a later subsection
Poisson regression was used to investigate the relation between skin tone and red cards received for research question 1
cases missing outcome, predictor, control, or exposure values were dropped (n=489), leaving a main analysis sample of N=1,564 unique players
total red cards received (M=1.01, SD=1.34) was entered as the outcome and total games played (M=237.73, SD=141.99) as a log-transformed exposure variable
unstandardized coefficients, robust standard errors, and odds ratios with 95% CIs for each predictor are reported in Table 1
robust standard errors were calculated using formulas provided by UCLA (2014)
an initial base model with only centered control variables (age, height, weight, goals scored) was evaluated first, so the intercept represents the 'average' player
dummy-coded France, Spain, Germany, and Forward/Midfielder/Fullback/Goalkeeper position variables were included as controls
the model intercept represented English players with position unavailable (missing position chosen as reference because it likely mixes all positions)
data on victories, ties, and defeats per player were not included as control variables because they were highly related to number of games played
the base model was significantly better than the null model at predicting outcome variability, Δχ2(11)=157.42, p<.001
red-card rate per game was related to league country and position played
an average player in France had a 46% higher red-card rate than in England (B=0.38, OR=1.46, 95%CI[1.21,1.76])
an average player in Spain had a 48% higher red-card rate than in England (B=0.40, OR=1.48, 95%CI[1.27,1.73])
playing in Germany showed little difference in red-card rate compared to England (B=-0.15, OR=0.86, 95%CI[0.73,1.02])
the average forward received only 66% as many red cards as the 'Other' position category (B=-0.42, OR=0.66, 95%CI[0.51,0.85])
the average midfielder received only 72% as many red cards as the 'Other' position category (B=-0.33, OR=0.72, 95%CI[0.57,0.90])
fullbacks did not demonstrate meaningful differences in red cards received relative to the reference category (B=0.10, OR=1.11, 95%CI[0.60,1.06])
player's age, height, weight, and number of goals scored did not relate meaningfully to red cards received
the skin tone variable was added as a predictor in a second step, after the control variables
the skin tone variable was not centered, since its values already ranged from 0 to 1

because skin tone was uncentered, the intercept represents the red-card rate for the lightest-rated players and the skin tone OR represents the increased rate for the darkest-rated players relative to lightest
adding skin tone significantly improved model fit versus the control-only model, Δχ2(1)=9.08, p=.003
skin tone showed a meaningful relation with red cards received (B=0.28, OR=1.32, 95%CI[1.06,1.63]): darkest-rated players received 32% more red cards per game than lightest-rated players

spans.note: Caveat that the confidence interval showed considerable variability around the skin tone effect estimate

spans.assertion: investigation of outliers, influential cases, residuals, and multicollinearity did not reveal violations of model assumptions
the model left a significant proportion of variability in red cards received unexplained (residual deviance=2007.23, df=1551, p<.001)
the significant unexplained residual deviance suggests other variables likely exist that are meaningfully related to red cards received
the data indicated a skin-tone-associated bias in red cards received, and players varied considerably in number of games played
after including games played as an exposure variable and controlling for league country and position, skin tone remained associated with more red cards for darker-skinned players
the second research question investigated the role of referee-home-country prejudice in the skin-tone/red-card bias relationship
technical difficulties again prevented use of mixed effects modeling, the preferred method, for research question 2
data was again aggregated at the unique-player level and Poisson regression was used to investigate factors related to red cards received
referee prejudice was represented by historical average implicit and explicit prejudice scores for the referee's home country
prejudice scores were weighted by games per player-referee dyad, summed at the player level, then divided by the player's total games to yield an average encountered-prejudice score
the resulting implicit (M=0.35, SD=0.02) and explicit (M=0.44, SD=0.11) prejudice scores had small standard deviations, making effect-size interpretation difficult
the implicit prejudice index was multiplied by 100 and the explicit prejudice index by 10 to address the small standard deviations

spans.note: Displayed equations for the implicit and explicit prejudice index calculations

spans.assertion: the same observations were excluded as in research question 1, arriving at the same final sample of N=1,564 unique players
the same base model with the same control variables from research question 1 was used
two separate models were developed to investigate implicit and explicit referee-home-country prejudice levels
centered main effects of skin tone and prejudice were entered in step 2, and a skin tone x prejudice interaction term was added in step 3

spans.note: Pointer stating results are presented in Table 2

spans.assertion: in the implicit-prejudice model, adding the main effects significantly improved fit over the control-only model, Δχ2(2)=17.02, p<.001
both main effects demonstrated meaningful associations with red cards received
darker skin tone was associated with more red cards relative to lighter skin tone in the implicit model (B=0.31, OR=1.36, 95%CI[1.09,1.69])
players encountering higher implicit referee prejudice received more red cards than those encountering lower levels (B=0.08, OR=1.08, 95%CI[1.02,1.15])
the skin tone x implicit prejudice interaction term was entered in the final model step
adding the skin tone x implicit prejudice interaction did not significantly improve model fit, Δχ2(1)=0.24, p=.63
the skin tone x implicit prejudice interaction term did not show a meaningful relation to red cards received (B=-0.03, OR=0.97, 95%CI[0.84,1.12])
in the explicit-prejudice model, adding the main effects again significantly improved fit over the control-only model, Δχ2(2)=15.28, p<.001
skin tone showed effect B=0.30, OR=1.35, 95%CI[1.09,1.67] in the explicit-prejudice model
explicit prejudice showed effect B=0.10, OR=1.11, 95%CI[1.02,1.21], the same relation pattern as the implicit model
adding the skin tone x explicit prejudice interaction did not significantly improve model fit, Δχ2(1)=0.39, p=.53
the skin tone x explicit prejudice interaction term did not show a meaningful relation to red cards received (B=-0.06, OR=0.94, 95%CI[0.76,1.17])
diagnostic checks of outliers, influential cases, residuals, and multicollinearity did not indicate violations of model assumptions
a significant amount of residual variability remained unexplained (residual deviance=1999.00, df=1549, p<.001)
players encountering referees from higher-prejudice countries (implicit or explicit) tended to receive more red cards than those encountering lower-prejudice referees
the referee-prejudice effect on red cards was independent of player's skin tone, and no skin tone x prejudice interaction was found for either implicit or explicit measures
skin tone bias in the awarding of red cards existed in the soccer games in the data set
age, height, weight, and goal-scoring ability did not appear meaningfully related to red cards received

skin tone showed a meaningful relation such that darker-skin-tone players tended to receive more red cards than lighter-skin-tone players, even after controlling for position, league country, and games played
the skin-tone bias was found independent of the average referee-home-country prejudice level the player encountered
the referee-prejudice statistic was not a direct measurement of the referees themselves, and the suboptimal technique used did not allow investigation of differences among individual referees

spans.note: Caveat that it would be premature to conclude referee prejudice played no role in the observed bias

spans.assertion: the specific prejudice variables used in the present analysis did not provide evidence for a role of referee prejudice
